source.title: Single-Agent Scaling Fails Multi-Agent Intelligence: Towards Foundation Models with Native Multi-Agent Intelligence
source.authors: Shu-Yue Hu; Hao Yan; Yi-Qun Zhang; Yang Chen; Dong-Zhan Zhou; Lei Bai

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendix tables are present. Some figure text is garbled in extraction, but the paper's written descriptions and regression statistics are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates how single-agent and multi-agent benchmark performance relates across model families, sizes, and generations, extending scaling-performance questions to multi-agent capabilities. It does not test the original held-out cross-entropy scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark accuracies and regressions relating single-agent task accuracy to multi-agent planning accuracy. Its discussion of loss scaling laws is background, not a measured result. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, training-token sweeps, compute-budget allocation experiments, or architecture-controlled comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. Scaling laws appear only as the counter-argument the authors set out to rebut. The measured results compare instruction-tuned checkpoints across generations at similar parameter counts, and regress multi-agent planning accuracy on single-agent benchmark accuracy. Neither result relates downstream performance to parameters, data, compute or pretraining loss, so V6 is not tested. No loss, compute or architecture results are reported, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested either. The finding concerns transfer between benchmark categories, a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that strong multi-agent intelligence will not emerge as a byproduct of single-agent capability gains. They call for deliberate work on datasets, evaluation, training (including population-based training) and safety.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares instruction-tuned model benchmark accuracies across families, sizes, and generations and fits regressions between task accuracies. It does not fit held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or optimize parameter-token allocations under compute budgets.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes differ by task category, model family, size group, and generation; the paper also reports substantial variation in multi-agent planning among models with similar single-agent task accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Across generations of Qwen and LLaMA instruction-tuned models at similar sizes, single-agent benchmark accuracy rises steeply. Multi-agent understanding rises modestly, and multi-agent planning (CoordinationQA) stays roughly flat or declines slightly. Log regressions of MA planning on SA accuracy are positive but noisy (R²≈0.61 Qwen, 0.58 LLaMA).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains in single-agent benchmark accuracy across model generations do not transfer proportionally to multi-agent coordination benchmarks.

record.problems: The comparison uses instruction-tuned checkpoints across generations, so differences in training, data, and other setup choices are not isolated. It reports benchmark accuracy rather than pretraining loss, and does not control compute or training-token budgets. The paper describes substantial cross-model variation; several plotted details are available only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: The appendix Tables 1 and 2 list many individual model scores across separate benchmarks. These were not expanded into individual rows because the claim-relevant findings summarized in the main text and Figure 3 are represented above; no results needed to be omitted to meet the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fits.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No analysis of downstream accuracy against parameter count, compute or pretraining loss. Within-generation size sweeps appear in the appendix tables but are not analysed.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (tests, T3) and its V6 limits_scope labels should be dropped. The experimental contrast is across generations at fixed size, or between two downstream benchmark categories, not scale or loss. Appendix Tables 1–2 contain within-generation size sweeps (e.g. Qwen2.5 0.5B→72B: MATH-500 0.290→0.838; CoordinationQA JP 0.129→0.347). These could in principle bear on V6, but the paper neither analyses nor fits them. A reviewer wanting V6 evidence would have to derive it themselves. The paper is a position paper with a small empirical section.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute-budget experiments or parameter/token allocation optima.
No controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures benchmark accuracy, not pretraining loss; its cross-model relationships do not isolate parameter-count scaling from generation, data, or training differences.
No comparison of loss-law exponents, fit choices, or compute-optimal splits.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses scaling laws as motivation for an argument about multi-agent competence; the experiments address a different relationship.

tranche.reason: The reported comparisons concern generations at similar parameter counts and MA accuracy versus SA accuracy. They do not evaluate any listed version's loss scaling, allocation, architectural invariance, or downstream prediction from scale or pretraining loss.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Figure labels are partly garbled, but the regression equations, statistics, surrounding explanations and checkpoint names needed for these checks are readable.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Single-agent accuracy rises substantially while multi-agent understanding improves more modestly and planning is mostly flat or sometimes declines (R1-R9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cross-model association between single-agent and multi-agent planning scores
reader_labels.reason: Both families show positive logarithmic associations, but the authors report substantial variation among models with similar single-agent accuracy, limiting predictability (R10-R11).
